title: This way, that way, any way
author: Melissa Muth Martinez
summary: Prompted by Michael Porter's line that a company without a strategy is willing to try anything, Muth Martinez argues that innovation without direction is a quiet source of dysfunction in mission-driven organizations. She grants that the urge to innovate is admirable, then redefines it as being about better rather than merely new. Six short scenarios illustrate the pattern: a goalless retreat, reactive crisis responses, a graveyard of project tools, a sudden flat structure, an overstuffed strategic plan and a startup that pivots weekly. Each ends with a one-line lesson about purpose, structure or clarity. She closes by rejecting the idea that strategy kills creativity and claims that sustainable innovation requires it.
points: Innovation is redefined as better and intentional, not simply new, which supplies a test for any proposed initiative.
When everything is fair game, nothing is a strategy, and teams end up reactive, incoherent and exhausted.
Rotating through project tools each year without an owner or defined use leaves only clutter.
Declaring a team flat without structure or decision rules produces chaos and disengagement rather than empowerment.
A strategic plan with dozens of priorities for a three-person team guarantees that little gets done.
quotes: Innovation isn't just about new—it's about better. It’s not just about iteration—it’s about intention.

I eventually began to understand that, when everything is fair game, nothing is a strategy. When we’re stuck in the mindset of “try anything,” we work from a place of reactivity, incoherence, and exhaustion.

There’s no agenda, no facilitation, and no objectives, because the goal is to get folks to be more “authentic.” After two days of surface-level icebreakers and vague discussions, the team’s feeling a lot of things, but trust isn’t one of them.

But because the root issues—internal issues around decision-making, accountability, classism, etc.—are never addressed, staff feel stuck in a performative loop of “trying anything,” never getting to a place where change feels possible.
But the organization has tried to do a complete 180 over night, with no structure, no shared language around decision-making processes, and no guardrails to help guide folks forward.
Staff feel kind of excited about the new direction for about a week, but then they realize there’s no world in which they could reasonably achieve what the strategic plan is outlining.
But the truth is: clarity isn’t the enemy of creativity; clarity can actually be the force that gives creativity direction and meaning.
